input:
This report presents the findings of an energy assessment that was carried out at the brewery, covering current energy use, the refrigeration system, the steam system, and a recommendation for action. The headline finding is that a heat-recovery retrofit applied to the refrigeration system is projected to save 16% of the brewery's electricity use, which corresponds to a derived saving of 660 MWh per year, worth $79,200 per year at the current price of $0.12 per kWh. Set against a capital cost of $244k, this gives a derived simple payback of 3.1 years. It should be noted at the outset that the steam figures used in this assessment are drawn from a single winter month and should therefore be regarded as seasonal in nature, whereas the electricity figures are based on a full year.

## Current use
Total electricity consumption at the brewery amounts to 4125 MWh per year, and refrigeration accounts for the largest share of this total; indeed, the refrigeration load is the load to which the projected saving of 16% applies. The remainder of the electricity is consumed by a variety of other users, including the brewhouse, the packaging operation, compressed air generation, lighting, and general site services, none of which individually comes close to the refrigeration load. The figure of 4125 MWh per year provides the baseline against which all of the savings discussed in this assessment are measured, and it is worth emphasising that this is a metered figure for a complete year rather than an estimate assembled from equipment nameplate ratings. Demand remains relatively steady throughout the year, since brewing continues in every month and both the cold store and the fermentation vessels require cooling on a continuous basis, with the main seasonal variation appearing on the steam side rather than in electricity consumption.

## Refrigeration
Refrigeration is comfortably the largest single consumer of electricity on the site, and it is also the source of the heat that the proposed retrofit would recover. The refrigeration plant rejects heat arising from the cold store, the fermentation vessels, and the packaged-product store, and at present this rejected heat is simply lost to the atmosphere. The proposed retrofit would recover heat from the refrigeration discharge and use it in duties for which the site currently generates heat separately. The projected saving of 660 MWh per year is a derived figure, obtained by applying the vendor's projected recovery to the refrigeration share of the total annual consumption of 4125 MWh, and it has not yet been demonstrated on an operating installation at this particular site. Its accuracy consequently depends on the refrigeration share and on the number of hours for which the plant operates under load, both of which vary over the course of the year.

## Steam
Steam is used in the brewhouse for a range of duties, of which wort boiling, cleaning, and pasteurisation account for the bulk of the consumption. The steam figures quoted in this assessment are taken from one winter month, which is the heaviest month of the year for steam demand, and they therefore overstate the annual average position by an amount that has not been corrected for in this report. Crucially, however, the recommendation does not depend on these steam figures, because the proposed retrofit acts on the refrigeration system and the associated saving is expressed in terms of electricity. Any interaction whereby recovered heat displaces steam generation is acknowledged to be real, but it has not been quantified here and has deliberately been excluded from the payback calculation rather than estimated.

## Recommendation
It is recommended that the brewery proceeds with the heat-recovery retrofit at a capital cost of $244k, with responsibility for delivery resting with the brewery engineering manager. The projected saving is 660 MWh per year, representing 16% of current electricity use, and at $0.12 per kWh this corresponds to a derived annual saving of $79,200, noting that 660 MWh is equivalent to 660,000 kWh. On this basis, the derived simple payback is 3.1 years. This payback is a simple one and makes no allowance for the maintenance of the additional equipment, for the time value of money, or for any future movement in the price of electricity, and it takes the vendor's projected saving at face value. It is further recommended that two checks are built into the delivery plan: firstly, that the refrigeration share of annual consumption is confirmed by sub-metering before any order is placed, and secondly, that the output of recovered heat is metered throughout the first year of operation so that the projected saving can be tested against a measured value.

The recommendation is approval to proceed, with the brewery engineering manager as owner. The steam figures in this assessment rest on one winter month and are treated as seasonal throughout; the electricity figures are annual and metered.

## Current use
Electricity use is 4125 MWh per year, and refrigeration takes the largest share of it. The remaining use is spread across the brewhouse, packaging, compressed air, lighting, and site services, none of which approaches the refrigeration load. Annual use of 4125 MWh is the base against which every saving in this assessment is measured, and it is a metered figure for a full year rather than an estimate built up from nameplate ratings. Demand is steady through the year by the standards of food and drink sites: brewing continues in every month, the cold store and the fermentation vessels call for cooling in every month, and the seasonal swing sits in the steam system rather than in electricity. No single end use besides refrigeration offers a saving of the size the retrofit addresses, which is why the assessment concentrates on the refrigeration plant and treats the other loads as background. The split between continuous and variable use matters for what follows. Much of the brewery's electricity runs whether or not beer is being packaged on a given day: refrigeration holds temperature continuously, and the cold store does not switch off between production runs. A measure that acts on a continuous load accumulates its saving over every hour of the year, which is part of the case for acting on refrigeration rather than on a load that runs only during production.

## Refrigeration
Refrigeration is the largest electricity consumer on the site and the source of the recoverable heat. The plant rejects heat from the cold store, the fermentation vessels, and the packaged-product store, and that rejected heat is currently lost to air. The retrofit recovers heat from the refrigeration discharge and puts it to work where the site now raises heat separately. The projected saving of 660 MWh per year is a derived figure: it is the vendor's projected recovery applied to the refrigeration share of the 4125 MWh annual use, and it has not been measured on an operating installation at this site. The saving is stated as 16% of electricity use, and its accuracy stands or falls with the refrigeration share and with the hours the plant runs loaded, both of which vary through the year. The recovered heat has a use on the same site at the same time. A brewery washes vessels, heats water, and warms spaces through the year, and the refrigeration plant rejects heat through the year as well; the match between a continuous source and a continuous demand is what makes the recovery practical rather than occasional. Where the recovered heat cannot be used at the moment it is produced, it is lost as surely as it is lost today, and the projected saving already stands or falls on the coincidence of the two profiles.

## Steam
Steam serves the brewhouse: wort boiling, cleaning, and pasteurisation draw the bulk of it. The steam figures in this assessment come from one winter month, the heaviest steam month of the year, and they overstate the annual average by an amount this assessment does not correct. The recommendation does not depend on the steam figures: the retrofit acts on the refrigeration system and its saving is stated in electricity. Where recovered heat displaces steam raising, the interaction is real but unquantified here, and it is excluded from the payback rather than estimated.

## Recommendation
The recommendation is to proceed with the heat-recovery retrofit at a capital cost of $244k, with the brewery engineering manager owning delivery. The projected saving is 660 MWh per year, 16% of current electricity use; at $0.12 per kWh the derived annual saving is $79,200 (660 MWh is 660,000 kWh), and the derived simple payback is 3.1 years on the capital cost. The payback is a simple payback: it takes no account of maintenance on the added equipment, of the time value of money, or of movement in the electricity price, and it holds the projected saving at its vendor figure. Two checks belong in the delivery plan: the refrigeration share of annual use is confirmed against sub-metering before the order is placed, and the recovered-heat output is metered through the first year so the projected saving is tested against a measured one. On those conditions the case rests on the electricity figures alone, which are annual and metered, and not on the seasonal steam figures. The decision the figures support is a decision to build, taken on metered electricity data and a vendor projection that the delivery plan then verifies. If the verification fails, the metering installed under the second check shows by how much, and the shortfall is a measured one rather than a suspicion.
